1:
Why the spoken word had now to be written is answered four ways. Henry gives four reasons: what was only spoken must be written that it might be reviewed and last longer; what was delivered at large with frequent repetitions must be contracted, that the parts might be compared; what they had heard once must be rehearsed, since what made no impression at first might take hold at the second hearing; and single sermons already published must be gathered into one volume that none be lost. Calvin argues from the fugitive nature of speech, since a hearer takes in only what his capacity allows and the words then glide away, whereas what is written can be weighed at leisure and read years after. Keil and Delitzsch deny that a collection was intended, holding the writing merely a means of presenting the whole contents once more, the prophet being prevented from going. Wesley makes it a memorial, so that the truth of the words might appear when the time came for their fulfilment.

What a roll of a book was draws out the antiquarians. Gill explains that sheets were glued together and rolled rather than cut and bound, whence the name volume, which we still keep for books that are nothing of the kind. Clarke describes the manufacture from copies lying before him, vellum or half-tanned sheepskin cut into lengths, stitched and wound on a roller, written in columns, sometimes carried on two rollers so that the reader coils with his right hand what he reads off with his left, as the law is still written for the synagogues. Calvin takes the word for the unwritten volume, blank when taken, and traces the Hebrew and Latin names alike to roots meaning to roll, adding that the old archives of his own country hold nothing but such rolls. Ellicott dates the phrase, which occurs in no earlier prophet or historical book and probably followed the coming in of parchment, the roll replacing the papyrus book whose fragile fabric needed a different form.

Why the prophet did not go himself is left unsettled. Calvin observes that sacred history records no imprisonment under this king, inclines to a restraint laid on him by God, and thinks it not improbable that after his earlier trial he had been forbidden the temple precincts. Ellicott agrees the hindrance was probably not imprisonment, since the two men could afterwards hide themselves, and notes that some months passed between the dictation and the reading, so that the scribe had to serve as preacher as well as amanuensis. Keil and Delitzsch say only that he was prevented from getting to the house.

The date connects the roll with what survives. Ellicott brings the message into close contact with an earlier chapter and infers that we have there the substance of part at least of what was dictated, its contents agreeing exactly with the description given here. Keil and Delitzsch fill in the year, in which the conqueror advanced after beating the Egyptians, took the city and made the king tributary, and argue that the command to write came only towards its end. Gill measures forward, eighteen years before the destruction.

Two voices go behind the dictation to the man dictating. Calvin holds that God suggested again what had slipped from the prophet's memory, since the greater part of so many words must otherwise have escaped him, so that he stood between God and the scribe. Ellicott finds a window into the workshop: the prophet speaks without premeditation as the word comes, a disciple reports and preserves the utterance, and from time to time the master collects, repeats, revises and edits what he has said. What the chapter records, he adds, is the history of the first volume of these discourses, which perished, though the book's earlier chapters are substantially a reproduction of it.
5:
Who proclaimed the fast is disputed, and the dispute matters. Henry gives it to the government without deciding whether king, princes or priests, and supposes the occasion the invading army or a want of rain. Ellicott gives it to the king on hearing the army was near, and adds a motive that changes the scene: the fast was probably called on the advice of the priests and false prophets, to rouse the people to a holy war of religious resistance, which would explain the prophet's eagerness to counteract the scheme with an unlooked-for sermon. Calvin gives it to the people, on the ground that the older versions and the Hebrew make them the subject, and that a king so ungodly would not have called it. Keil and Delitzsch answer that the people cannot have called it, since those from the country towns came up only in consequence of its being appointed, and report the suggestion that the phrase is used generally of keeping a fast.

Why that day was chosen is agreed, and doubled by one. Clarke calls it a favourable time for such tremendous prophecies, since multitudes would be gathered from all parts to implore mercy; Wesley says the same, the prophet choosing it for the concourse; Ellicott adds that the courts would be more than usually thronged and the people more disposed to listen. Calvin gives a second reason the others leave out: a fast was enjoined to supplicate mercy and deprecate wrath, so the day itself ought to have left them submissive and teachable, prepared to take a threatening calmly. He notes too that the prophet did not shelter behind his scribe, telling him to read from the volume rather than report from memory.

How long the roll lay written before it was read is variously reckoned. Gill sets the first reading in the seventh month of the fourth year and this in the ninth of the fifth, which looks like fourteen months, then corrects himself, since counting from the spring makes the interval only two. Henry supposes the writing may have taken the best part of a year, or only a month or two, and thinks the scribe had already read to smaller companies before this most solemn reading of the whole. Ellicott prefers the Hebrew year to the one the Greek gives, allows an interval of some months, and suggests the substance was meanwhile made known to the inner circle of disciples.

Why the prophet was shut up is answered by canvassing. Gill reports the reading that he was in prison and rejects it, since an order to arrest him afterwards would then have been needless; reports another that the king had confined him to his house; and offers two of his own, a restraint of the Spirit or some legal pollution unfitting him for the courts. Keil and Delitzsch put it no further than that he was prevented from getting to the house.

The scribe's obedience closes the tile. Gill notes that he observed the charge punctually as to things, time and place. Calvin commends the promptitude, since the office was dangerous and the message very disagreeable, and the man made no refusal; he adds that the words are called the Lord's here and the prophet's a little later without change of meaning, since God is represented by his ministers and often transfers to them what belongs peculiarly to himself. On the falling of the supplication, Gill and Clarke keep the physical image, the prostrated body and dejected countenance of men falling down to deplore their sins. Calvin joins prayer and conversion as both necessary, since a man who seeks reconciliation in words only will not succeed, then guards the joining, since a sinner might repent a thousand times and remain exposed to judgment: pardon rests not on repentance but on the gratuitous mercy that embraces him.
10:
Why the son of Gemariah carried the report down to the palace is the open question. Gill weighs ill will against good will and prefers the second, since the man brings no charge and his father afterwards joins those who plead against the burning of the roll. Ellicott holds it obvious from the relation between them that the purpose was not unfriendly, and suspects a preconcerted plan between the prophet and his friends, the report giving an opening to bring the scribe before the king's counsellors. Calvin declines to decide: the man may have been an informer ingratiating himself as courtiers do, which would show that not all who hear patiently are teachable; or he may have been filled with wonder and carried up what he thought incredible.

The chamber is placed and its owner traced. Keil and Delitzsch make him a secretary of state, probably brother to the man who had earlier protected the prophet, and set the chamber in the upper court at the entrance of a gate whose position cannot now be fixed. Ellicott takes the family as the point, three generations of devout patriotism: the father worked with the high priest on the restoration of the house, published the contents of the newly found book of the law and probably ordered copies made; one son protected the prophet, and this son lends his chamber to the prophet's delegate; the gate may have been part of the father's building work, which would explain a chamber over it falling to the son.

The messenger sent to fetch the scribe has an unusually long pedigree. Ellicott reads its two ends, since the last name means Ethiopian and belonged to an alien turned proselyte, while the law admitted such a man's descendants to full incorporation only in the third generation, so the name meaning Jew fell naturally to the child who first became entitled to it. Keil and Delitzsch report two scholars who take both names for appellatives on the same ground.

What the princes felt is measured differently. Ellicott finds a conflict of feelings, alarm for themselves and their country at woes they half believed, and alarm for the two men bold enough to utter them; they had no hostile purpose, but the matter had come to their official knowledge and they had no alternative but to report it. Calvin allows the fear was real enough for them to seat the scribe respectfully, but marks the turning of one to another as the sign that it was not genuine, since a man who fears rightly examines himself before God while a wavering mind looks about it; their care not to offend the king he calls the religion of the court, fearing God just so far as not to lose favour. Gill notes that they heard patiently, which the king afterwards would not. Clarke has them convinced the prophecy was from God and anxious to save both men, yet obliged to inform.

The question they put about the writing is not thought idle, though Gill admits it may look odd at first sight. Clarke repoints the clause to make the sense whether the scribe had copied the words or written them as they were prophesied. Calvin has the counsellors suspecting trickery, since they could hardly believe such a quantity had been delivered from memory, and observes that the answer takes the two questions in reverse order, as Scripture often does. Keil and Delitzsch get it from the tense, which expresses continued action and so means dictation, a thing requiring much time, the clause showing the scribe did nothing else throughout but write. Wesley draws the consequence the others leave implicit, that this could only add to their fear, since without a special influence of God it had been impossible to recall all that was spoken at several times over so many years.
20:
That the princes left the roll behind is read three ways. Ellicott makes it an official precaution: if either man were prosecuted the document had to be available for reference, and lodging it with the keeper of the archives shows they already feared what the king did, so they reported the substance from memory. Calvin makes it courtly timidity, since there is no independence at court and the greatest flatterer stands highest, so men who would not offend tender ears carried a report rather than the thing itself; their regard for God, he adds, was small and frigid, for if they believed the roll came from the Spirit the king's displeasure should not have weighed so much. Gill sees protocol, that they would first send to learn whether the king could be spoken with.

Henry watches who was made to read it. Not the scribe, who could have read it with more authority and affection than anyone; not one of the princes, to whom it would have been no disparagement; least of all the king himself; but the page then in waiting, who perhaps scarcely knew how to make sense of it. Those who despise the word of God so, he adds, soon show that they hate it too.

The setting is filled in from the season. Clarke describes the winter apartment as suited to a month when snow often lies there, and the fire as a brazier of coals, the rich burning wood in brass or earthen pans set anywhere in the room while the poor burn sticks on the floor.

What was cut, and by whom, gets the closest work. Gill offers the glued breadths or the columns, and reports a rabbinic view that verses of the Lamentations are meant. Clarke settles for columns, since the sacred books are written in them and the word denotes the openings between them, and calls the blade the scribe's own knife. Keil and Delitzsch make them divisions rather than leaves and reject the inference that it was a leaved book, since the synagogues still use true rolls wound on a stick with the text divided into parts. Ellicott grants that the English suggests a papyrus book while the Hebrew will bear either sense, and observes that the Hebrew leaves it as uncertain as the English whether the king cut and burned the roll himself or the reader did it with his approval, though the next verse favours the king. He calls the act childish impatience betraying anger, and thinks the king could not bear to hear of the seventy years, which would have stood in an early column.

The absence of horror is what they dwell on. Keil and Delitzsch contrast an earlier king who rent his garments in a like case, and separate the court attendants who felt nothing from the princes who had been alarmed, against a scholar who identified the two and marred the sense. Gill reports the Jewish rule drawn from this verse, that a man who sees the book of the law cut to pieces should rend his own. Calvin speaks as one astonished and says the simple statement carries more force than any invective: that mortals should not be moved when God fulminates, but grow harder, is a diabolical madness and a sign of reprobation. Three princes did intercede, which Wesley credits to a greater dread of God, and Calvin turns into an aggravation, since men drawn back by others and persevering still are the less excusable. On the arrest, Gill doubts the king would send his own son and takes the name for a servant's; Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch read a member of the royal house, the king having been too young at his accession to have a grown son. Clarke and Wesley agree the search failed because God did not permit it.
27:
Why the burned roll was written again is worked hardest by Calvin. He observes that God has another way with the rebellious, sometimes ceasing to speak and judging in silence when he sees his labour spent in vain; here he chose the opposite, because the king had foolishly supposed that a power reduced to ashes was extinguished with the parchment, whereas the word cannot be bound. The renewed threatening, he adds, came not in hope of benefit but to expose the madness to ridicule. Clarke notes that no duplicate had been kept, so the same matter had to be given again, with the heavy judgment on the king now added. Ellicott places the command during the concealment and thinks we owe to it the present form of an earlier chapter.

The sentence that no successor should sit is qualified, since a son did reign. Ellicott states fact and answer together, that the boy-prince held a tributary throne three months only and the next king was a brother, not a son. Calvin works the Hebrew, which says not that none shall sit but that none shall be to him, so the exclusion is of his own posterity; the three months went uncounted, and the uncle who followed was set up by the conqueror out of ill-will, to degrade the two he displaced. Wesley puts it shortest, that none should reign any considerable time. Clarke takes the harder line, no successor at all and an untimely end without burial, and draws the moral that a man who destroys the evidence against him only doubles his punishment.

The unburied body gets a reason as well as a sentence. Calvin points out that the threat alone would not have produced the effect intended, so the cause is stated, that king and counsellors and people alike had been forewarned in good time and none had repented; there would have been hope had they deprecated the wrath, and it is the despising of the threatening that makes the iniquity extreme. Gill ties the punishment to the act, the cutting and burning done by the king or by his order, with his sons perhaps looking on pleased and his servants assenting, three excepted. Ellicott notes that the same prediction stands in an earlier chapter, probably written after this.

Calvin alone attends to the naming. The title of king is given, he says, not for honour but to show how vainly he gloried in it, since the prophet had been set over nations and kingdoms and sent to reprove mountains and hills, and no elevation in the world could intercept prophetic truth. He reads the clause as encouragement to the prophet as much as sentence on the king, lest a high position terrify the man who had to deliver it.

What became of the enlarged roll closes it. Ellicott finds the verse showing the genesis of the present volume, since the discourse delivered in the temple court was revised and enlarged, dictated to the same scribe, and in that shape has probably come down to us. Clarke supposes the additions were threatenings of temporary importance and local application, which the Spirit did not think proper to record. Calvin turns to the man who dictated, whose constancy he thinks deserves no common praise, since he had lately fled in fear and knew the king had ordered him killed, and yet went on to exasperate him further; the prophets were not exempt from fear and were often anxious for their safety, but preferred the duty laid on them to their lives. As for why the second roll cost nobody anything, he answers that the king was not changed and did not spare them out of kindness, but that God, when he does not soften the hearts of the ungodly, still bridles their violence so they cannot find the way to do what they wish.
